findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL/NoSQL Injection
findings.description: The login endpoint is vulnerable to authentication bypass through SQL/NoSQL injection. An attacker can use crafted payloads in the email field to log in as any user, including administrators, without knowing their password.
findings.recommendation: Implement strict input validation and use parameterized queries or ORMs with proper escaping for all database interactions. Avoid dynamic query construction with user-supplied input.

findings.title: Usage of Known Vulnerable JavaScript Libraries
findings.description: The application uses several outdated JavaScript libraries (e.g., AngularJS 1.x, jQuery 2.x, Bootstrap 3.x) that contain known security vulnerabilities. Exploitation could lead to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), DOM manipulation, or other client-side attacks.
findings.recommendation: Update all third-party JavaScript libraries and frameworks to their latest stable versions. Regularly audit dependencies for known vulnerabilities using tools like OWASP Dependency-Check or Snyk.

findings.title: Sensitive Directory Listing Enabled
findings.description: The `/ftp` directory is accessible and allows directory listing, exposing potentially sensitive files such as `coupons_2013.md.bak` or `package.json`. This can provide attackers with valuable information about the application's structure, configuration, or internal data.
findings.recommendation: Disable directory listing for all web server directories. Ensure that sensitive files and directories are not publicly accessible and are properly secured or removed from the web root.

findings.title: Directory Traversal via /ftp endpoint
findings.description: The '/ftp' endpoint appears to be vulnerable to directory traversal, allowing access to arbitrary files outside the intended directory. This could lead to sensitive information disclosure (e.g., /etc/passwd) or potentially remote code execution if combined with other vulnerabilities.
findings.recommendation: Implement strict input validation and sanitization for file paths. Ensure that no user-supplied input is directly used to construct file paths without proper canonicalization and validation against an allow-list of safe directories. Restrict access to files within a specific, controlled directory.

findings.title: Missing Content Security Policy (CSP)
findings.description: The application at juice-shop.herokuapp.com does not implement a Content Security Policy (CSP) header. A CSP is a security standard that helps prevent various types of attacks, including Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection by specifying which dynamic resources are allowed to load. Without a CSP, the application is more vulnerable to malicious content injection and execution if other vulnerabilities (like XSS) are present, allowing attackers greater control over the browser's behavior.
findings.recommendation: Implement a robust Content Security Policy (CSP) header. Start with a strict CSP that allows resources only from trusted sources (e.g., 'self', specific CDNs). Monitor the CSP using report-only mode initially to identify legitimate violations before enforcing it. Example: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.com; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'self'; upgrade-insecure-requests;` This policy should be tailored to the application's specific needs.

findings.title: SQL Injection on 'id' parameter
findings.description: The 'id' GET parameter on the 'juice-shop.herokuapp.com' application is vulnerable to SQL Injection. This allows an attacker to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the backend database, potentially leading to data exfiltration, modification, or even remote code execution depending on the database configuration and underlying operating system privileges. The application does not properly sanitize user-supplied input before incorporating it into SQL queries, leading to this critical vulnerability.
findings.recommendation: Implement strong input validation and sanitization for all user-supplied input, especially for parameters used in database queries. Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) or Object-Relational Mappers (ORMs) that automatically handle SQL escaping. Avoid dynamic query construction using string concatenation. Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) as an additional layer of defense.

findings.title: TLS 1.0 Protocol Enabled
findings.description: The server supports TLS 1.0. This version of the Transport Layer Security protocol is deprecated and considered insecure due to known vulnerabilities like BEAST. Modern security standards (e.g., PCI DSS) require disabling it, and major browsers have dropped support.
findings.recommendation: Disable TLS 1.0 on the server. Configure the server to only support TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Ensure that all clients connecting to the server are capable of using these newer, more secure protocols.

findings.title: TLS 1.1 Protocol Enabled
findings.description: The server supports TLS 1.1. While an improvement over TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 is also deprecated and lacks support for modern cryptographic algorithms and features. It is no longer considered secure by industry standards and organizations like NIST, PCI DSS, and major browser vendors.
findings.recommendation: Disable TLS 1.1 on the server. Configure the server to only support TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Ensure that all clients connecting to the server are capable of using these newer, more secure protocols.

findings.title: Dev Subdomain Exposure
findings.description: The 'dev' subdomain is publicly accessible, potentially exposing development-specific configurations, unpatched vulnerabilities, or sensitive information not intended for production environments. This could include debugging tools, verbose error messages, or access to development databases.
findings.recommendation: Restrict public access to development environments using IP whitelisting or VPN. Ensure no sensitive data or credentials are present in development codebases. Implement strict access controls and regular security audits for all non-production environments.

findings.title: API Endpoint Discovery
findings.description: A dedicated API endpoint has been discovered, indicating the presence of a programmatic interface for the application. APIs often have different authentication mechanisms and can be a target for various attacks such as broken access control, injection flaws, or rate limiting bypasses if not properly secured.
findings.recommendation: Conduct a thorough penetration test specifically targeting the API. Ensure robust authentication and authorization mechanisms are in place. Implement API rate limiting, input validation, and secure error handling. Document the API thoroughly and follow OWASP API Security Top 10 guidelines.

findings.title: Admin Panel Exposure
findings.description: An 'admin' subdomain has been identified, suggesting the presence of an administrative interface. Public exposure of an admin panel poses a critical risk, as unauthorized access could lead to full control over the application, data manipulation, or system compromise.
findings.recommendation: Immediately restrict access to the admin panel using strong authentication, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and IP whitelisting. Implement robust logging and monitoring for all administrative activities. Ensure the admin panel is not directly accessible from the internet without proper controls.

findings.title: Test Environment Exposure
findings.description: A 'test' subdomain is publicly discoverable. Test environments often contain outdated software, default credentials, or simplified security configurations, making them easier targets for attackers. They might also expose internal network structures or unreleased features.
findings.recommendation: Restrict public access to test environments. Ensure test environments are isolated from production and do not contain real sensitive data. Implement the same security standards as production environments or decommission them when not in use.

findings.title: CORS Wildcard
findings.description: The server responds to cross-origin requests with the header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *', indicating that any domain can make requests to this endpoint. This 'wildcard' configuration might allow malicious websites to interact with the application's resources or user data, potentially leading to data leakage or unauthorized actions if sensitive information or authenticated sessions are accessible via this endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header to a specific list of trusted domains that genuinely require cross-origin access. Avoid using '*' unless the resource is intended to be publicly accessible without any sensitive data or state. If CORS is not strictly required, remove the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header entirely.

findings.title: S3 Bucket Publicly Accessible
findings.description: An S3 bucket containing static assets and potentially sensitive configuration files for juice-shop.herokuapp.com is publicly readable via anonymous access. This could expose application structure, unversioned secrets, or allow for content enumeration.
findings.recommendation: Restrict S3 bucket access to authenticated users or specific IP ranges. Enable block public access settings at the bucket and account level. Review bucket contents for any sensitive data that might have been inadvertently stored.

findings.title: RDS Database Instance Publicly Accessible
findings.description: The production RDS MySQL database instance for juice-shop.herokuapp.com is configured with a public IP address and accessible from the internet. This significantly increases the attack surface for the database.
findings.recommendation: Place the RDS instance in a private subnet. Use a bastion host or VPN for administrative access. Restrict inbound traffic to the database security group to only necessary application servers.

findings.title: IAM Role with Excessive Permissions
findings.description: The IAM role 'JuiceShopAppRole' used by the juice-shop application has 'AdministratorAccess' or similarly broad permissions (e.g., 's3:*', 'ec2:*'), violating the principle of least privilege. A compromise of the application could lead to full control over AWS resources.
findings.recommendation: Review and narrow down IAM role permissions to only what is absolutely necessary for the application to function. Implement granular, resource-specific policies.

findings.title: GCP Cloud Storage Bucket Publicly Accessible
findings.description: A Google Cloud Storage bucket named 'juice-shop-logs-prod', potentially containing application logs or backups for juice-shop.herokuapp.com, is publicly readable. This could expose sensitive operational data or personal information.
findings.recommendation: Restrict bucket access to specific service accounts or users. Ensure uniform bucket-level access is enabled. Implement appropriate IAM policies to limit public exposure.

findings.title: Unrestricted Security Group Ingress on SSH
findings.description: A security group associated with the juice-shop web servers allows inbound SSH traffic (port 22) from anywhere (0.0.0.0/0). This exposes the EC2 instances to brute-force attacks and potential unauthorized access.
findings.recommendation: Restrict inbound SSH access to specific, trusted IP ranges (e.g., internal networks, VPN IPs). Implement a bastion host or use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager for secure server access without direct SSH exposure.

findings.title: K8s Dashboard Exposed
findings.description: The Kubernetes Dashboard, a web-based UI for managing cluster applications, is exposed externally to the internet without proper authentication or authorization. This misconfiguration allows potential attackers to gain administrative control over the Kubernetes cluster, deploy malicious workloads, or exfiltrate sensitive data, severely compromising the entire environment hosting juice-shop.herokuapp.com.
findings.recommendation:
1. Implement strict network policies (e.g., NetworkPolicies, security groups) to restrict access to the Kubernetes Dashboard only from trusted internal networks or specific IP ranges.
2. Configure strong Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) policies to limit user permissions, ensuring the principle of least privilege.
3. Consider disabling external access entirely and using a secure VPN or an identity-aware proxy for internal access.
4. Ensure the Dashboard is running the latest version with all security patches applied and remove default service account tokens from being used.

findings.title: BOLA / IDOR
findings.description: The `/api/v1/users/{id}` endpoint is vulnerable to Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). An unauthorized user can access sensitive information of other users by manipulating the `id` parameter in the URL path. By changing the `id` from their own user ID to another, an attacker can retrieve details such as email addresses, names, and potentially other personal data belonging to other users, including administrators, without proper authorization checks.
findings.recommendation: Implement robust authorization checks for all object-level access. Ensure that a user can only access resources (like user profiles) that they are explicitly authorized to view or modify. This typically involves verifying the user's identity and their permissions against the requested resource's owner or associated roles. Always validate the ownership of the requested resource against the authenticated user's session.

findings.title: Cloudflare WAF Detected
findings.description: Cloudflare is a widely used content delivery network (CDN) and web application firewall (WAF) service. Its WAF provides protection against various web-based attacks such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and DDoS attacks by filtering malicious traffic before it reaches the origin server.
findings.recommendation: The presence of a WAF indicates an active layer of defense. However, it does not guarantee complete immunity from all vulnerabilities. Further security testing should be conducted to identify potential bypasses for the WAF or underlying application vulnerabilities. For defensive teams, ensure Cloudflare WAF rules are appropriately configured, regularly updated, and monitored for alerts.

findings.title: SQL Injection Vulnerability on Login Page
findings.description: The application's login endpoint is vulnerable to SQL Injection. An attacker can bypass authentication by manipulating the 'email' parameter, gaining unauthorized access to the application. This vulnerability also allows for the enumeration of database schema, tables, and sensitive user data, directly compromising user identities and privacy.
findings.recommendation: Implement parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database interactions. Avoid dynamic SQL query construction. Validate and sanitize all user input before processing. Employ a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to detect and block common attack patterns.

findings.title: Subdomain Takeover
findings.description: A subdomain takeover vulnerability exists for 'shop.juice-shop.herokuapp.com'. This occurs because the subdomain's DNS CNAME record points to an external service (e.g., Heroku, AWS S3, GitHub Pages) that is no longer active or has been deprovisioned. An attacker can register the external service's resource (in this case, a Heroku application named 'non-existent-app-for-takeover') and gain full control over the 'shop.juice-shop.herokuapp.com' subdomain. This allows the attacker to host arbitrary content, potentially leading to phishing attacks, cookie theft, defacement, content injection, and other malicious activities, leveraging the trust associated with the main domain 'juice-shop.herokuapp.com'.
findings.recommendation: Immediately remove the dangling DNS CNAME record for 'shop.juice-shop.herokuapp.com' that points to 'non-existent-app-for-takeover.herokuapp.com'. If the subdomain is still required, update the CNAME record to point to an active and properly managed resource under your control. Implement a regular review process for all DNS records to ensure they are valid and correspond to active services. Establish a clear procedure for removing DNS entries when external services are deprovisioned or no longer in use.
